# Malnutrition in older adults: a wider view

**Authors:** C. Finn McQuaid; Madhavi Bhargava; Pranay Sinha; Anurag Bhargava; Rein M.G.J. Houben

**Affiliations:** 1TB Modelling Group, TB Centre and Centre for Mathematical Modelling of Infectious Diseases, Department of Infectious Disease Epidemiology, London School of Hygiene & Tropical Medicine, London, UK | 2Department of Community Medicine, Yenepoya Medical College, Mangalore, India | 3Center for Nutrition Studies, Yenepoya University, Mangalore, India | 4Section of Infectious Diseases, Department of Medicine, Boston University Chobanian & Avedisian School of Medicine, Boston, USA | 5Department of Medicine, Yenepoya Medical College Hospital, Mangalore, India | 6Department of Medicine, McGill University, Montreal, QC, Canada

As Dent and colleagues note, malnutrition is an important and widely prevalent determinant of health in older adults1. They also highlight the importance of its management in older adults affected by COVID-19. However, we find missing the link to tuberculosis (and other infectious diseases that are more prevalent in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs)). Tuberculosis is a known driver of wasting and continues to kill over one and a half million people each year.2

Tuberculosis is perhaps the best example of the bi-directional relationship between malnutrition and infectious diseases. It is an important, and potentially reversible, driver of two of the three phenotypic criteria in the Global Leadership Initiative on Malnutrition: unintentional weight loss and low body mass index.3 Conversely malnutrition also leads to tuberculosis, with one in five cases of tuberculosis directly attributable to undernutrition, increasing to at least one in three in countries like India.4 The malnutrition-tuberculosis interaction is heightened in older LMIC populations with higher prevalence of both, and reduced access to care exacerbating an already challenging situation.2

In high tuberculosis burden countries, the majority of which are LMICs, any older adult with malnutrition on screening needs to be evaluated for tuberculosis as an underlying cause. Reciprocally, nutritional assessment and management for older adults with tuberculosis is vital to ensure favourable treatment outcomes.5 Given the interaction with other diseases and high burden of malnutrition in older populations in LMICs, taking a wider, Global Health-centric view is warranted, and that should include TB.
